Random Forest - Bank Customers’ Perceptions

Random Forest- What is it?

Random Forest is a machine learning algorithm based on the idea of combining many simple models to obtain a more robust result. Specifically, it builds multiple decision trees (a “forest”) and aggregates their outputs to produce more stable and accurate predictions.

In market research, Random Forest can be applied to both regression and classification problems, such as predicting satisfaction, recommendation, or churn. It is also used in combination with cluster analysis, either to explain segment membership or to identify the key variables that differentiate segments. By handling complex, non-linear relationships, Random Forest complements traditional exploratory techniques and supports more robust, data-driven decision making.

Dataset and Survey Example

The data used in this example are purely synthetic and serve illustrative purposes only.

Segmentation case

For the following example, we are going to use a formerly calculated 6 cluster solution based on k-means clustering:

As shown in the chart, the six-cluster solution reveals clearly differentiated customer profiles. Cluster 1 (20%) includes individuals who score slightly below average overall, but place relatively greater importance on safety and brand reputation. This segment is labelled “Safety-first”. Cluster 2 (14%) is primarily driven by the online banking experience and represents digitally oriented customers, here referred to as “Digital customers”. Cluster 3 (24%) shows consistently low scores across all items and reflects the least engaged group with the bank; this segment is labelled “Disengaged”. Cluster 4 (18%), while sharing some similarities with digital customers, places its strongest emphasis on customer support and is therefore referred to as “Support-seeking”. Cluster 5 (7%) emerges as the most demanding segment, with above-average evaluations across all dimensions, and is labelled “All-in customers”. Finally, Cluster 6 (17%) also shows generally above-average scores, with a particularly strong focus on attractive savings and loan products, and is referred to as “Product-oriented”.

Random Forest Classification

In this section, the confusion matrix is used to examine how well the identified customer segments can be distinguished from one another. Rather than evaluating prediction accuracy in a strict sense, the goal is to understand whether the clusters represent clearly differentiated profiles or whether some degree of overlap exists between them.

The matrix is read by comparing rows and columns. Each row represents the true segment a customer belongs to, while each column represents the segment predicted by the model. Values along the diagonal indicate customers who are correctly classified within their original segment, whereas values outside the diagonal show cases where customers are confused with another segment. For each cluster, the classification error indicates the share of customers that are not clearly distinguished from other groups.

  • Safety-first (7% error) Most customers in this segment are correctly classified (105 out of 113). Misclassification is limited and mainly occurs with Product-oriented and Disengaged customers, suggesting some shared characteristics but overall a well-defined safety-driven profile.

  • Digital customers (8% error) Digital customers are classified accurately in most cases (71 out of 77). When misclassification occurs, it is almost exclusively with Product-oriented customers, indicating some overlap between digital usage and interest in financial products.

  • Disengaged (3% error) This is the most clearly defined segment, with 130 out of 134 customers correctly classified. The very low error rate reflects a strong and consistent low-engagement profile that is easy to distinguish from other segments.

  • Support-seeking (7% error) Most Support-seeking customers are correctly identified (95 out of 102). Limited confusion with Digital and Product-oriented customers suggests some overlap in service expectations, while customer support remains the key differentiator.

  • Highly demanding (15% error) This segment shows a higher error rate, with 33 out of 39 customers correctly classified. Misclassification occurs mainly with Product-oriented customers, indicating blurred boundaries between highly demanding profiles and strong product expectations.

  • Product-oriented (19% error) Product-oriented customers show the highest classification error, with 79 out of 98 correctly classified. Confusion with Digital and Highly demanding customers suggests that product focus often coexists with other priorities, making this segment broader and less sharply defined.

The Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) quantifies the agreement between two groupings while correcting for chance, with values closer to 1 indicating stronger agreement.

The chart shows a two-dimensional MDS projection of customers in the holdout sample, coloured according to the segment predicted by the Random Forest model. Each point represents a customer, while the shaded areas indicate the outer boundaries of each segment. The visualization highlights how some segments are clearly separated, while others partially overlap, reflecting natural similarities between certain customer profiles rather than sharp, artificial boundaries.

Random Forest Variable Importance

Random Forest models are especially useful for marketing applications that require understanding which variables matter most. By building many trees using different subsets of predictors, Random Forest can handle wide datasets with a large number of variables. Variable importance is assessed by randomly permuting the values of each variable and measuring how much model performance drops: important variables lead to a noticeable decrease in accuracy, while unimportant ones have little or no effect.

The chart shows the relative importance of each variable in distinguishing between customer segments, based on the Random Forest model. Each point represents a variable, with higher values indicating a stronger contribution to separating customers into different segments. Variables appearing at the top of the chart play a more influential role in the segmentation, while those lower down contribute less to differentiating customer profiles.

From a decision-making perspective, the results suggest that not all attributes contribute equally to differentiating customer segments. Variables such as high-quality customer support and an enjoyable online banking experience emerge as key drivers, indicating that improvements in service quality and digital experience are likely to have the greatest impact on how customers are segmented. In contrast, attributes like perceived safety of money or a wide range of banking products show relatively low importance, suggesting they function as baseline expectations rather than sources of differentiation. For strategic planning, this implies that banks should prioritize investments in customer support and digital channels to create meaningful differentiation, while maintaining—rather than over-investing in—hygiene factors such as safety and product breadth.

We now explore importance of variables segment by segment:

The segment-level variable importance charts show which factors are most effective at distinguishing each segment from the rest of the customer base. For each segment, variables with higher importance values represent the attributes that most strongly define its uniqueness relative to other groups. These drivers highlight where each segment differs most from the overall population, rather than simply reflecting average preference levels. From a decision-making perspective, this enables more targeted strategies by identifying the specific levers that can be used to address, retain, or reposition customers within each segment.
